Introducing Veo 3, our video generation model with expanded creative controls – including native audio and extended videos.

Improved prompt adherence, meaning more accurate responses to your instructions.
Offers new levels of control, consistency, and creativity – now across audio.

It excels at quickly turning text prompts and images into short videos, and lets you refine results across multiple turns using the Interactions API.
multi-input reasoning (supporting text, images, audio, and video inputs simultaneously), character consistency... multi-turn conversational editing (e.g., element replacement or perspective changes)

Not as impressive as Sora: Sora's clips were long with lots of rapid movement, while Veo's shots are only a few seconds long and almost all look like slow motion or slow panning, seemingly cherrypicked for little movement. The one comparable cyberpunk video looked 'crazy inconsistent.'
It's mildly interesting how many of the samples shown fail to fully conform to the prompts. Lots of specifics are missing, though Google was transparent about it.
Complaints about access at launch: you had to sign in just to see a demo, it was a waitlist rather than a release, and the VideoFX/ImageFX links were down or not working.
Veo 3: 'Blown away at how well the audio/video matches up, and the dialogue is better sounding / on-par with dedicated voice models.'
Wow, the audio integration really makes a huge difference, especially given it does both sounds and voices.
Like most AI video tools, the results look good at first glance, but the more you watch, the more flaws and sloppiness you notice, and they really lack storytelling.
'Ehh, really for $20.' Break dancers with no music, people just pop in and out. How would anyone use this for a commercial application?
Doesn't look better than the initial Sora release. Output is still smooth, shiny, floaty and robotic, and recognizably AI-generated.

Professional tools have outpaced open source: Wan and Hunyuan are solid free options, but the latest from Google and Runway feel a league above. The biggest differentiator is editing tools (prompting motion, direction, cuts, audio).

Veo 2 winning 2:1 in user preference vs Sora Turbo is impressive, but it has similar limitations: leg swapping in the ice skating video, and the beekeeper lifting the jar with unnatural acceleration. Maybe slightly better at natural movement and physics than Sora.

Got preview access. For 'A pelican riding a bicycle along a coastal path,' only two outputs showed a pelican riding a bicycle; others showed one running, one on a stationary bike. 'All four were better than what I got from Sora.'
The skateboarding video is wildly unrealistic whenever he performs a trick, with just morphing body parts. Some of the other videos look incredibly believable, though.
Is it just me or do all these models generate everything in a weird pseudo-slow motion framerate?

Questions real use beyond 10-second demos: can it produce multiple shots with continuity of faces, backgrounds and lighting for even a 60-second commercial? Google's own note that consistency in complex scenes 'remains a challenge' suggests not.
'VideoFX isn't available in your country yet.' Several users also reported the Veo 2 page crashing or struggling on iPad Chrome, iPhone and Brave iOS.
Amazing that something as computationally expensive as generating 8-second videos is available in Gemini/Whisk, outside a paid API.
Burned through $48 in GCP credit making 12 eight-second videos in Veo 2. Beware.

Content moderation is frustrating: animating a cartoon of themselves drinking coffee via veo-2.0-generate-001 was blocked, and another user said 'I just want to make some fun videos where my kid plays a superhero, but it keeps failing.'
Whisk's video generation redraws the entire source picture so it barely resembles the original; asked for a tool that doesn't change the image so much.
Even the curated 'Glacial Cavern' demo misses the prompt: the candy figures aren't within the ice walls. Great if you don't care about all requirements, but frustrating when exactness matters.

The demo videos are pretty neat and would have impressed four months earlier, but they are underwhelming next to the Sora demo, especially coming from Google, which owns the largest video collection in the world.

Shots are only a few seconds long and mostly slow-motion or slow panning, apparently cherry-picked to avoid hard movement. The one comparable fast cyberpunk clip 'looks crazy inconsistent', unlike Sora's real-speed walking videos.

GPT-4o shipped while Veo got a waitlist. Users called it a half-baked release unavailable in most countries, with confusing Veo vs VisionFX sign-up messaging and repeated sign-in prompts just to see a demo.

Questioned Google's rater comparison: Veo samples were 8s while most competitors' were 5s. Raters might simply prefer longer videos, so Veo 2 output should have been trimmed to 5s for a fair test.

Winning 2:1 in preference over Sora Turbo is impressive and it may emulate physics slightly better, but it shares Sora's limitations: legs swap in the ice skating video and the beekeeper's jar pops up with unnatural acceleration.
